Modern Chess960 openings

There is a theory out there that it may be possible to study openings in Chess960. I disagree. To study even the first move to make in each and every Chess960 position would require far more study than studying, say, even a complex opening like the Sicilian Najdorf in depth.

To give people an idea of what it would be like to study opening theory in Chess960, I present this document. This document, generated by having Stockfish18 analyze the opening setups (at a 21-ply depth) has all 960 Chess960 opening positions, sorted by how balanced the position is (positions with the lowest advantage for White are shown first).

For each position, I show White’s best move(s), along with other good moves for White. In addition, since it’s popular to have “pie rule” with other abstract games, where one person chooses White’s first move and the other person gets to choose whether they are Black or White, I also show moves, for each position, that are as balanced as possible for White and Black.

As one can see, it’s very unlikely anyone will ever memorize openings for Chess960 they way they do with Classic Chess. And, if it were possible for a human to memorize openings for all 960 positions, we can then simply play Double Fischer Random Chess instead, where the White and Black starting positions are independently randomly chosen, and use computer analysis to make sure the resulting setup is balanced for both sides. A study of all 921,600 possible Double Fischer Random positions done a few years ago found over 14,000 balanced positions—far beyond any human’s ability to memorize openings. Indeed, Double Fischer Random results in more balanced positions that Chess960 can make.

Notable positions

  • The most balanced position: RQKBNNBR
  • The least balanced position: BBRQKRNN
  • Chess18 positions, where the rooks are in the corners, and the king is on the e file: RBBQKNNR (This position goes back to 1868 when Augustus Mongredien held a Chess tournament with this particular setup) RQNBKNBR RNQBKNBR RBBNKNQR RBNQKNBR (This position was played in 1875 between Blackbourne and Potter, and annotated by future world Chess champion Steinitz) RBQNKNBR RQBNKBNR RNBQKBNR (Classic Chess) RQNNKBBR RBBNKQNR RNNQKBBR RBNNKQBR RNBBKNQR RQBBKNNR RNQNKBBR RNNBKQBR RNBBKQNR RNBNKBQR
  • Classic Chess
